[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"API Security and OAuth2/OIDC Protocols"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Modern API Security"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) form the backbone of modern web applications, microservices, and mobile apps. Securing these interfaces is critical because they often expose sensitive business logic and data backends directly to the internet. Unlike traditional monolithic web applications, APIs are stateless and rely heavily on token-based authentication mechanisms."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding OAuth 2.0"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that enables applications to obtain limited access to user accounts on an HTTP service. It works by delegating user authentication to the service that hosts the user account, and authorizing third-party applications to access the user account. OAuth 2.0 introduces several key roles: the Resource Owner, Resource Server, Client, and Authorization Server."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Resource Owner: The user who grants access to their protected resource."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Client: The application requesting access to the resource owner's account."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Authorization Server: The server issuing access tokens to the client after successfully authenticating the resource owner."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Resource Server: The server hosting the protected resources, capable of accepting and validating access tokens."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"The Authorization Code Flow with PKCE"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"For public clients such as mobile apps and Single Page Applications (SPAs), the Authorization Code Flow with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is the industry standard. PKCE prevents authorization code interception attacks by introducing a dynamically created cryptographically random key called the code verifier."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.com%2Fcallback&scope=read%2Awrite&code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrGMTJguCHivQFR1SWNXYAg5X0lQoZw&code_challenge_method=S256 HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"OpenID Connect (OIDC) Layer"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"While OAuth 2.0 handles authorization, it does not handle authentication or identify the user. OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0. It introduces the ID Token, a JSON Web Token (JWT) that securely communicates information about the authenticated user."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"{
  "iss": "https://auth.example.com",

  "aud": "s6BhdRkqt3",
  "nonce": "n-0S6_WzA2Mj",
  "exp": 1311281970,
  "iat": 1311280970,
  "name": "Jane Doe",
  "email": "janedoe@example.com"
}"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Securing APIs"},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always enforce HTTPS to protect tokens and sensitive data in transit from man-in-the-middle attacks."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use short-lived access tokens combined with secure refresh token rotation strategies."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Implement robust scope validation and granular role-based access control (RBAC) on the resource server."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Apply strict rate limiting to authentication endpoints to mitigate brute-force and denial-of-service attempts."}]
